Error in s_ldsc(traits = traits, sample.prev = sample.prev, population.prev = population.prev,  :

Here is what I ran

                     sample.prev=sample.prev,
                     population.prev=population.prev ,
                     ld=ld,
                     wld=wld,
                     frq=frq,
                     trait.names = trait.names)
Alex

messages.body_plain:
It's still not very clear what your model is and whether it includes individual SNPs or not.
That said, we do not typically recommend changing LDSC intercepts.
You should be able to tell from documentation what was used to produce the sumstats. I wouldn't move forward with an analysis without knowing where they came from both in terms of participants and GWAS pipeline.
Some of those intercepts are indeed high, although if the mean chisqs are very high, then I suppose this is not as worrisome.
Are some of your phenotypes created by merging (e.g. averaging) other phenotypes? That could create a singular matrix.

Sorry, I started at the end.
1. Running the Common Factor GWAS model (skipped the non-SNP models, but will do today).
2.  I am looking at 4 liver function enzymes GWAS - ALT, ALP, AST, and GGT -, from the Neale Lab UKB pipeline.  Looks like Neale Lab used linear regression (in HAIL) for all pipeline GWAS, and not BOLT-LMM.  I used the standardized quantile phenotypes, rather than raw phenotypes.  All phenotypes were measured in U/L, then standardized.  These would be distinct enzymes levels in blood.
3. I ran the GWAS model by chromosome - 20 of 22 ran.
4. Question - would there be something to look for (duplicate values maybe ), some line number for the error code, something so I don't have to go through 380000 lines from p_sumstats? In my first look (scrolling through data), I saw 2 lines, 2 snps, but same values across the line (beta.ggt, se.ggt, beta.ast, se.ast, etc).

Again, thanks for any help.

Dan

messages.subject: Re: negative STD_genotype
messages.body_plain:
Hi Joel,
I'm not sure what the issue is. What you show is that for the parameter in question there is a negative estimate as well as a negative standardized parameter estimate. If the parameter is a regression, covariance, or factor loading then this simply means that there is a negative association of some sort. If the parameter is a variance or residual variance, then it is out-of-bounds but this can happen depending on the data and the model specified. It simply is the weighted least squares estimate for the parameter given the model and the data. Whether this is a serious issue or not will depend on the entire model, the full set of parameter estimates, and what you are trying to accomplish in your analysis.

messages.subject: Re: Retaining SNPs in sumstats
messages.body_plain:
You would need to impute each sample to the same reference panel and redo the Univariate GWASs…

Otherwise you are in the same territory that is common for cross-referencing hits across GWASs where you might do something like find a proxy SNP for a variant of interest that isn’t genotypes or imputed..

I can think of more creative solutions off the top of my head but we haven’t tested or implemented those.

messages.subject: Re: LDSC I matrix
messages.body_plain:
Hi Daniel,

Again, I would not recommend manually changing elements of the I matrix (or any other elements of the LDSC output) unless you are a very advanced user, if at all. The diagonals of I are mostly used for diagnostics. The diagonals of I also used to correct standard errors of SNP effects for models with SNPs. If you do not want to correct the SEs for potential inflation indicated by a univariate LDSC intercept >1.0, you do not need to set the diagonals of I to 1. You can simply set (GC) Genomic Control to none (https://github.com/GenomicSEM/GenomicSEM/wiki/4.-Common-Factor-GWAS). Note that the off-diagonals of I are used to estimate the degree of shared estimation error across GWAS sumstats, and are therefore crucial for obtaining correct SEs and p values in multivariate GWAS within Genomic SEM.

I can't provide specific guidance on whether to be concerned by a univariate intercept that departs from 1.0. The degree of departure will depend on unmodeled popstrat along with sample size (i.e. GWAS power).  It is common to examine the ratio of the mean chisq-1 to the univariate LDSC intercept-1 to get a sense of how much polygenic signal there is relative to confounding. There isn't a canonical paper on this, apart from the original Bulik-Sullivan paper so you'll need to familiarize yourself with a range of recent GWAS papers. I'm not sure why you would get a univariate intercept substantially less than 1.0 unless N is low, there is some sort of overcorrection for pop strat, or a nontraditional GWAS was conducted. In the latter case, we cannot provide specific recommendations.

Elliot
